Zophar rebukes Job (verses 1–6)

Zophar attacked Job forcefully.

He portrayed him as someone who enjoyed hearing himself speak despite having nothing useful to say, and who defended lies.

Zophar wished God would show Job that his punishment was actually less than he deserved.

In our disputes, we are often too eager to call upon God to intervene.

We assume that if he spoke, he would certainly agree with our side.

We should submit every disagreement to the Lord's judgment, because his judgment accords with truth.

But those most eager to invoke divine judgment are not necessarily the ones who are right.

Zophar speaks about God's greatness (verses 7–12)

Zophar spoke well about God's greatness and glory and human folly and vanity.

We should recognize our own weakness and be humbled.

God sees the foolishness of human beings who want to become wise and be recognized as wise, though their hearts are like an untamed wild donkey's colt.

Human beings are empty and foolish, yet proud of themselves.

They desire the appearance of wisdom without submitting to wisdom's laws.

They reach for knowledge God has forbidden.

Like the first parents, they try to become wise beyond what has been written and lose the tree of life through seeking the tree of knowledge.

How can a creature in this condition claim to argue on equal terms with God?

Zophar promises good if Job repents (verses 13–20)

Zophar urged Job to repent and offered encouragement.

Yet even this counsel was mixed with harsh assumptions about Job.

Zophar believed prosperity in this life always belonged to the righteous.

He thought Job should be considered a hypocrite unless worldly prosperity returned.

Zophar said Job could lift his face without stain.

In Henry's spiritual application, people may approach the throne of grace confidently rather than with the fear Job described earlier (Job 9:34).

When God looks upon us through his Anointed One, our downcast faces can rise.

Though once polluted, we can be washed by Christ's blood and presented without stain.

We can draw near in full assurance of faith when our hearts have been cleansed from guilty consciences (Hebrews 10:22).
classic_reading:
[Job.11.1-Job.11.6]
Chapter 11
Chapter Outline
Zophar reproves Job. | (1-6) |
God's perfections and almighty power. | (7-12) |
Zophar assures Job of blessings if he repented. | (13-20) |
Verses 1-6
Zophar attacked Job with great vehemence. He represented him as a man that loved to hear himself speak, though he could say nothing to the purpose, and as a man that maintained falsehoods. He desired God would show Job that less punishment was exacted than he deserved. We are ready, with much assurance, to call God to act in our quarrels, and to think that if he would but speak, he would take our part. We ought to leave all disputes to the judgment of God, which we are sure is according to truth; but those are not always right who are most forward to appeal to the Divine judgment.
[Job.11.7-Job.11.12]
Verses 7-12
Zophar speaks well concerning God and his greatness and glory, concerning man and his vanity and folly. See here what man is; and let him be humbled. God sees this concerning vain man, that he would be wise, would be thought so, though he is born like a wild ass's colt, so unteachable and untameable. Man is a vain creature; empty, so the word is. Yet he is a proud creature, and self-conceited. He would be wise, would be thought so, though he will not submit to the laws of wisdom. He would be wise, he reaches after forbidden wisdom, and, like his first parents, aiming to be wise above what is written, loses the tree of life for the tree of knowledge. Is such a creature as this fit to contend with God?
[Job.11.13-Job.11.20]
Verses 13-20
Zophar exhorts Job to repentance, and gives him encouragement, yet mixed with hard thoughts of him. He thought that worldly prosperity was always the lot of the righteous, and that Job was to be deemed a hypocrite unless his prosperity was restored. Then shalt thou lift up thy face without spot; that is, thou mayst come boldly to the throne of grace, and not with the terror and amazement expressed in ch. 9:34. If we are looked upon in the face of the Anointed, our faces that were cast down may be lifted up; though polluted, being now washed with the blood of Christ, they may be lifted up without spot. We may draw near in full assurance of faith, when we are sprinkled from an evil conscience, [Heb.10.22] He 10:22.

Job rebukes his friends (verses 1–5)

Job criticized his friends for thinking their wisdom was so much greater than his.

We often mistake correction for insult and imagine we are being mocked when someone offers advice or warning.

That is our own folly.

But here Job had some reason to object.

He suspected his friends treated him this way because poverty and suffering had lowered his social standing.

This is how the world often behaves.

Even upright people may be despised when troubles overshadow their lives.

Wicked people often prosper (verses 6–11)

Job appealed to observable facts.

Bold robbers, oppressive people and those who openly despise God often enjoy prosperity.

Yet this is not simply chance.

The Lord governs these things.

Worldly prosperity has little value in his sight.

He has better gifts for his children.

Job referred everything to God's complete ownership of every created thing.

He asked his friends to let him consider and assess their claims, appealing to any fair judgment.

Job celebrates God's wisdom and power (<reference osisRef="Job.12.12-Job.12.25" resp="BibleResourcesOriginalSourceRangeInModernSectionHeading">verses 12–25</reference>)

Here Job gave a noble account of God's wisdom, power and sovereignty.

The Lord governs all human affairs according to the counsel of his will.

No one can resist him.

Wise and godly people who disagree about lesser matters would do well to dwell chiefly on the great truths they share.

Doing so brings honor, comfort and benefit to themselves and to others.

Here Job offered neither accusations nor complaints.

He described numerous ways God rules human affairs, overruling every scheme and overcoming every opposition.

Possessing all wisdom and power, God knows how to use even foolish and wicked people.

If he did not govern the world, so much foolishness and dishonesty would have brought it to ruin long ago.

These truths should have made Job and his friends recognize that they were out of their depth when claiming to know why God had afflicted Job.

God's ways are beyond searching, and his judgments cannot be fully traced.

Scripture contains many wonderful examples of divine wisdom in sovereignty.

But the greatest and most important is the crucifixion of Jesus Christ—which Henry attributes to what he calls “the malice of the Jews.”

Only God could have known that this terrible act would become the salvation of the world.
classic_reading:
[Job.12.1-Job.12.5]
Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
Job reproves his friends. | (1-5) |
The wicked often prosper. | (6-11) |
Job speaks of the wisdom and power of God. | (12-25) |
Verses 1-5
Job upbraids his friends with the good opinion they had of their own wisdom compared with his. We are apt to call reproofs reproaches, and to think ourselves mocked when advised and admonished; this is our folly; yet here was colour for this charge. He suspected the true cause of their conduct to be, that they despised him who was fallen into poverty. It is the way of the world. Even the just, upright man, if he comes under a cloud, is looked upon with contempt.
[Job.12.6-Job.12.11]
Verses 6-11
Job appeals to facts. The most audacious robbers, oppressors, and impious wretches, often prosper. Yet this is not by fortune or chance; the Lord orders these things. Worldly prosperity is of small value in his sight: he has better things for his children. Job resolves all into the absolute proprietorship which God has in all the creatures. He demands from his friends liberty to judge of what they had said; he appeals to any fair judgment. ( [Job.12.12-Job.12.25] Job 12:12-25)
[Job.12.12-Job.12.25]
Verses 12-25
This is a noble discourse of Job concerning the wisdom, power, and sovereignty of God, in ordering all the affairs of the children of men, according to the counsel of His own will, which none can resist. It were well if wise and good men, who differ about lesser things, would see how it is for their honour and comfort, and the good of others, to dwell most upon the great things in which they agree. Here are no complaints, or reflections. He gives many instances of God's powerful management of the children of men, overruling all their counsels, and overcoming all their oppositions. Having all strength and wisdom, God knows how to make use, even of those who are foolish and bad; otherwise there is so little wisdom and so little honesty in the world, that all had been in confusion and ruin long ago. These important truths were suited to convince the disputants that they were out of their depth in attempting to assign the Lord's reasons for afflicting Job; his ways are unsearchable, and his judgments past finding out. Let us remark what beautiful illustrations there are in the word of God, confirming his sovereignty, and wisdom in that sovereignty: but the highest and infinitely the most important is, that the Lord Jesus was crucified by the malice of the Jews; and who but the Lord could have known that this one event was the salvation of the world?

Job challenges his friends' claims (verses 1–12)

Job spoke too highly of himself when he insisted that his friends had nothing to teach him.

Those who argue are tempted to magnify themselves and belittle others.

Whenever fear of judgment, spiritual temptation or suffering overwhelms us, we should turn to the Physician of our souls.

He rejects no one, never prescribes the wrong remedy and never leaves a case without a cure.

We may speak to him whenever we need.

For broken hearts and wounded consciences, every created comfort without Christ is an ineffective physician.

Job spoke to his friends in unmistakable anger.

His friends had expressed some truths that were relevant to Job, but an unhumble heart does not receive human correction gently.

Job expresses confidence in God (verses 13–22)

Job resolved to stand by his conscience's witness to his integrity.

He relied on God for justification and salvation, the two great blessings we hope for through Christ.

Job expected little in the way of earthly deliverance.

But he remained confident concerning his eternal salvation.

He believed God would not only save him and make him happy but also be his salvation, the One whose presence and enjoyment would be his happiness.

He knew he was not a hypocrite and concluded that God would not finally reject him.

We should be satisfied to have God as our Friend, even at times when his dealings seem those of an enemy.

We must trust that all things will work for our good, even when everything appears to be against us.

Cling to God even when he gives no immediate sense of comfort.

In the hour of death, seek living comfort from him.

This is what it means to trust him though he slays us.

Job asks God to reveal his sins (verses 23–28)

Job wanted his sins to be made known to him.

A genuinely repentant person is willing to know the worst about personal wrongdoing.

We should all desire to see our transgressions clearly so that we can confess them and avoid them in the future.

Job lamented how severely God seemed to deal with him.

Time does not erase the guilt of sin.

When God brings bitter things to our remembrance, he may intend us to recall neglected sins and turn from them.

Young people should beware of indulging sin.

Even in this life, moments of sinful pleasure can produce months of sorrow.

It is far wiser to remember the Creator in youth and gain an assured hope and a peaceful conscience that will comfort us in later years.

Job also complained that his present missteps seemed to be examined with excessive strictness.

But God does not treat us according to what our sins deserve.

Job's complaint arose from a gloomy view of his circumstances.

If God strictly examined our steps and paths in judgment, both body and soul would feel his righteous vengeance.

That will be the dreadful condition of unbelievers.

But salvation has been planned, provided and revealed in Christ.
classic_reading:
[Job.13.1-Job.13.12]
Chapter 13
Chapter Outline
Job reproves his friends. | (1-12) |
He professes his confidence in God. | (13-22) |
Job entreats to know his sins. | (23-28) |
Verses 1-12
With self-preference, Job declared that he needed not to be taught by them. Those who dispute are tempted to magnify themselves, and lower their brethren, more than is fit. When dismayed or distressed with the fear of wrath, the force of temptation, or the weight of affliction, we should apply to the Physician of our souls, who never rejects any, never prescribes amiss, and never leaves any case uncured. To Him we may speak at all times. To broken hearts and wounded consciences, all creatures, without Christ, are physicians of no value. Job evidently speaks with a very angry spirit against his friends. They had advanced some truths which nearly concerned Job, but the heart unhumbled before God, never meekly receives the reproofs of men.
[Job.13.13-Job.13.22]
Verses 13-22
Job resolved to cleave to the testimony his own conscience gave of his uprightness. He depended upon God for justification and salvation, the two great things we hope for through Christ. Temporal salvation he little expected, but of his eternal salvation he was very confident; that God would not only be his Saviour to make him happy, but his salvation, in the sight and enjoyment of whom he should be happy. He knew himself not to be a hypocrite, and concluded that he should not be rejected. We should be well pleased with God as a Friend, even when he seems against us as an enemy. We must believe that all shall work for good to us, even when all seems to make against us. We must cleave to God, yea, though we cannot for the present find comfort in him. In a dying hour, we must derive from him living comforts; and this is to trust in him, though he slay us.
[Job.13.23-Job.13.28]
Verses 23-28
Job begs to have his sins discovered to him. A true penitent is willing to know the worst of himself; and we should all desire to know what our transgressions are, that we may confess them, and guard against them for the future. Job complains sorrowfully of God's severe dealings with him. Time does not wear out the guilt of sin. When God writes bitter things against us, his design is to make us bring forgotten sins to mind, and so to bring us to repent of them, as to break us off from them. Let young persons beware of indulging in sin. Even in this world they may so possess the sins of their youth, as to have months of sorrow for moments of pleasure. Their wisdom is to remember their Creator in their early days, that they may have assured hope, and sweet peace of conscience, as the solace of their declining years. Job also complains that his present mistakes are strictly noticed. So far from this, God deals not with us according to our deserts. This was the language of Job's melancholy views. If God marks our steps, and narrowly examines our paths, in judgment, both body and soul feel his righteous vengeance. This will be the awful case of unbelievers, yet there is salvation devised, provided, and made known in Christ.

Job reflects on human life (verses 1–6)

Job continued reflecting on the human condition while also addressing God.

Every descendant of fallen Adam has a short life.

Human beauty, happiness and splendor vanish before disease or death, like a flower cut down or a shadow fading away.

How can a person's conduct be entirely free from sin when the heart is unclean by nature?

Henry regards this as clear evidence that Job understood original sin.

Job seems to have raised this truth to ask God to treat him not according to his own works, but according to mercy and grace.

God has determined how long each of us will live.

Our times are in his hands, and natural processes operate under his rule.

In him we live and move.

Remembering how brief and uncertain life is, and how quickly earthly pleasures fade, can help us greatly.

But even more important is to understand the cause and the remedy of our condition.

Until the Holy Spirit gives us new birth, nothing spiritually good dwells in us or comes from us.

Even the little good performed by regenerated people remains mixed with sin.

We should therefore humble ourselves and depend entirely upon God's mercy through our divine Surety, Christ.

Seek the Holy Spirit's daily renewal and look toward heaven as the only place of perfect holiness and happiness.

Job considers death and resurrection (verses 7–15)

A tree that has been cut down may sprout again if water is available.

A human being who dies, however, is permanently removed from the former place in this world.

Human life resembles floodwaters that spread widely and then quickly dry up.

Henry understands Job's words as expressing belief in the resurrection.

Job's friends had proved such miserable comforters that he turned toward the hope of a future change.

If our sins have been forgiven and our hearts made holy, heaven will be our souls' rest.

Meanwhile our bodies will lie hidden in the grave, no longer harmed by enemies or troubled by the corruption and discipline of earthly life.

Job struggles with sin, suffering and mortality (verses 16–22)

At moments Job's faith and hope became stronger and the work of grace appeared renewed.

But soon his remaining sinful nature prevailed again.

He spoke as though God had pushed his judgment to the furthest extreme against him.

The Lord will prevail against everyone who tries to contend with him.

God may send disease and pain, remove the companionship of those we love and take away every earthly hope.

Yet he will receive the believer into eternal happiness.

What a different end awaits the prosperous unbeliever when summoned before God's judgment seat!

The Lord still sits upon a throne of mercy, ready to show grace.

May sinners consider their final end while there is still time.

The body that human beings hesitate to lay aside may suffer intensely near death.

The soul they hesitate to surrender may experience sorrow.

Dying can be difficult work and death's pain severe.

It is foolish to postpone repentance until a deathbed, when weakness may make the one most necessary task difficult to perform.
classic_reading:
[Job.14.1-Job.14.6]
Chapter 14
Chapter Outline
Job speaks of man's life. | (1-6) |
Of man's death. | (7-15) |
By sin man is subject to corruption. | (16-22) |
Verses 1-6
Job enlarges upon the condition of man, addressing himself also to God. Every man of Adam's fallen race is short-lived. All his show of beauty, happiness, and splendour falls before the stroke of sickness or death, as the flower before the scythe; or passes away like the shadow. How is it possible for a man's conduct to be sinless, when his heart is by nature unclean? Here is a clear proof that Job understood and believed the doctrine of original sin. He seems to have intended it as a plea, why the Lord should not deal with him according to his own works, but according to His mercy and grace. It is determined, in the counsel and decree of God, how long we shall live. Our times are in his hands, the powers of nature act under him; in him we live and move. And it is very useful to reflect seriously on the shortness and uncertainty of human life, and the fading nature of all earthly enjoyments. But it is still more important to look at the cause, and remedy of these evils. Until we are born of the Spirit, no spiritually good thing dwells in us, or can proceed from us. Even the little good in the regenerate is defiled with sin. We should therefore humble ourselves before God, and cast ourselves wholly on the mercy of God, through our Divine Surety. We should daily seek the renewing of the Holy Ghost, and look to heaven as the only place of perfect holiness and happiness.
[Job.14.7-Job.14.15]
Verses 7-15
Though a tree is cut down, yet, in a moist situation, shoots come forth, and grow up as a newly planted tree. But when man is cut off by death, he is for ever removed from his place in this world. The life of man may fitly be compared to the waters of a land flood, which spread far, but soon dry up. All Job's expressions here show his belief in the great doctrine of the resurrection. Job's friends proving miserable comforters, he pleases himself with the expectation of a change. If our sins are forgiven, and our hearts renewed to holiness, heaven will be the rest of our souls, while our bodies are hidden in the grave from the malice of our enemies, feeling no more pain from our corruptions, or our corrections.
[Job.14.16-Job.14.22]
Verses 16-22
Job's faith and hope spake, and grace appeared to revive; but depravity again prevailed. He represents God as carrying matters to extremity against him. The Lord must prevail against all who contend with him. God may send disease and pain, we may lose all comfort in those near and dear to us, every hope of earthly happiness may be destroyed, but God will receive the believer into realms of eternal happiness. But what a change awaits the prosperous unbeliever! How will he answer when God shall call him to his tribunal? The Lord is yet upon a mercy-seat, ready to be gracious. Oh that sinners would be wise, that they would consider their latter end! While man's flesh is upon him, that is, the body he is so loth to lay down, it shall have pain; and while his soul is within him, that is, the spirit he is so loth to resign, it shall mourn. Dying work is hard work; dying pangs often are sore pangs. It is folly for men to defer repentance to a death-bed, and to have that to do which is the one thing needful, when unfit to do anything.

Eliphaz criticizes Job again (verses 1–16)

Eliphaz began his second attack upon Job.

Instead of becoming gentler after hearing Job's suffering, he became harsher.

He wrongly accused Job of abandoning reverence for God, neglecting prayer and losing all regard for the Lord.

Henry summarizes much of religion in two duties: fearing God as a vital inward principle, and praying to God as a vital practice.

Eliphaz also charged Job with conceit and with despising the advice and comfort his friends offered.

We often imagine our own words are of great importance when others, sometimes with good reason, find little value in them.

Eliphaz accused Job of resisting God himself.

Yet he should not have placed such harsh interpretations upon the words of someone long known for godliness and now enduring temptation.

These speakers clearly recognized original sin and the deep corruption of fallen human nature.

But that true doctrine did not make their harsh accusations against Job just.

Let us marvel at God's patience in enduring sinners.

Let us marvel even more at his love in redeeming us through his beloved Son, Jesus Christ.

Eliphaz describes the unrest of wicked people (verses 17–35)

Eliphaz correctly taught that wicked people are in a miserable condition.

But from that truth he drew a false conclusion: because Job was miserable, Job must be wicked.

The fact that some of God's people prosper in the world does not mean those who experience poverty or loss cannot also belong to him.

Eliphaz described the anxiety of wicked people, especially oppressors.

Such people often live in fear and die in misery.

If the prosperity of unrepentant sinners ends in ruin, we should regard other people's disasters as warnings.

God's correction does not feel pleasant while we undergo it.

Nevertheless, it can produce the peaceful fruit of righteousness in those who learn from it.

No hardship, however severe, can rob a true follower of the Lord of his favor.

What can separate us from Christ's love?
classic_reading:
[Job.15.1-Job.15.16]
Chapter 15
Chapter Outline
Eliphaz reproves Job. | (1-16) |
The unquietness of wicked men. | (17-35) |
Verses 1-16
Eliphaz begins a second attack upon Job, instead of being softened by his complaints. He unjustly charges Job with casting off the fear of God, and all regard to him, and restraining prayer. See in what religion is summed up, fearing God, and praying to him; the former the most needful principle, the latter the most needful practice. Eliphaz charges Job with self-conceit. He charges him with contempt of the counsels and comforts given him by his friends. We are apt to think that which we ourselves say is important, when others, with reason, think little of it. He charges him with opposition to God. Eliphaz ought not to have put harsh constructions upon the words of one well known for piety, and now in temptation. It is plain that these disputants were deeply convinced of the doctrine of original sin, and the total depravity of human nature. Shall we not admire the patience of God in bearing with us? and still more his love to us in the redemption of Christ Jesus his beloved Son?
[Job.15.17-Job.15.35]
Verses 17-35
Eliphaz maintains that the wicked are certainly miserable: whence he would infer, that the miserable are certainly wicked, and therefore Job was so. But because many of God's people have prospered in this world, it does not therefore follow that those who are crossed and made poor, as Job, are not God's people. Eliphaz shows also that wicked people, particularly oppressors, are subject to continual terror, live very uncomfortably, and perish very miserably. Will the prosperity of presumptuous sinners end miserably as here described? Then let the mischiefs which befal others, be our warnings. Though no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous, nevertheless, afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruits of righteousness to them that are exercised thereby. No calamity, no trouble, however heavy, however severe, can rob a follower of the Lord of his favour. What shall separate him from the love of Christ?

Job calls his friends miserable comforters (verses 1–5)

Eliphaz had claimed Job's words were useless and irrelevant.

Job now made the same charge against Eliphaz's words.

People who condemn others' speech should expect their own to be condemned in turn.

This is easy, and the exchange can continue indefinitely.

But what good does it accomplish?

Angry replies excite passions. They do not convince minds or make truth clearer.

Job's judgment of his friends also reminds us of the limits of every created comfort compared with God.

Eventually we will all discover that without him, created things are poor comforters.

When sin weighs on the conscience, judgment terrifies or death approaches, the Holy Spirit alone can give truly effective comfort.

In times of suffering, all other comfort without his work accomplishes little.

We should sympathize deeply with the sorrows of our brothers and sisters, as if they were our own.

Soon enough, those troubles may become our own.

Job describes his misery (verses 6–16)

Job gave a painful account of his suffering.

How much reason do we have to thank God if we are not experiencing troubles like his!

Even good people find it hard, during great distress, to prevent bitter thoughts about God.

Eliphaz had accused Job of refusing humility.

Job replied that he understood humility all too well: dust was the right place for him.

In this he reminds us of Christ, the Man of Sorrows, who pronounced mourners blessed because they would receive comfort.

Job defends his innocence and seeks a witness (verses 17–22)

Job's position was terrible.

Yet his conscience testified that he had not willingly practiced any grave, deliberate sin.

He remained ready to acknowledge sins arising from human weakness.

Eliphaz had accused him of religious hypocrisy.

Job therefore pointed to prayer, a central act of true religion, and maintained that his prayers had been sincere, though not free from every imperfection.

He still had a God to whom he could turn, confident that the Lord fully knew his suffering.

People who pour out tears before God may have many faults and be unable to defend themselves.

Yet they have a Friend who pleads for them—the Son of Man.

Our hope of acceptance before God must rest upon him.

Death is a journey from which we do not return to earthly life.

Each of us must make that journey, certainly and soon.

Should the Savior not therefore be precious to us?

Should we not be prepared to obey and suffer for him?

If our consciences have been cleansed by his atoning blood and testify that we are not continuing deliberately in sin or hypocrisy, death will become release from prison and entrance into everlasting joy.
classic_reading:
[Job.16.1-Job.16.5]
Chapter 16
Chapter Outline
Job reproves his friends. | (1-5) |
He represents his case as deplorable. | (6-16) |
Job maintains his innocency. | (17-22) |
Verses 1-5
Eliphaz had represented Job's discourses as unprofitable, and nothing to the purpose; Job here gives his the same character. Those who pass censures, must expect to have them retorted; it is easy, it is endless, but what good does it do? Angry answers stir up men's passions, but never convince their judgments, nor set truth in a clear light. What Job says of his friends is true of all creatures, in comparison with God; one time or other we shall be made to see and own that miserable comforters are they all. When under convictions of sin, terrors of conscience, or the arrests of death, only the blessed Spirit can comfort effectually; all others, without him, do it miserably, and to no purpose. Whatever our brethren's sorrows are, we ought by sympathy to make them our own; they may soon be so.
[Job.16.6-Job.16.16]
Verses 6-16
Here is a doleful representation of Job's grievances. What reason we have to bless God, that we are not making such complaints! Even good men, when in great troubles, have much ado not to entertain hard thoughts of God. Eliphaz had represented Job as unhumbled under his affliction: No, says Job, I know better things; the dust is now the fittest place for me. In this he reminds us of Christ, who was a man of sorrows, and pronounced those blessed that mourn, for they shall be comforted.
[Job.16.17-Job.16.22]
Verses 17-22
Job's condition was very deplorable; but he had the testimony of his conscience for him, that he never allowed himself in any gross sin. No one was ever more ready to acknowledge sins of infirmity. Eliphaz had charged him with hypocrisy in religion, but he specifies prayer, the great act of religion, and professes that in this he was pure, though not from all infirmity. He had a God to go to, who he doubted not took full notice of all his sorrows. Those who pour out tears before God, though they cannot plead for themselves, by reason of their defects, have a Friend to plead for them, even the Son of man, and on him we must ground all our hopes of acceptance with God. To die, is to go the way whence we shall not return. We must all of us, very certainly, and very shortly, go this journey. Should not then the Saviour be precious to our souls? And ought we not to be ready to obey and to suffer for his sake? If our consciences are sprinkled with his atoning blood, and testify that we are not living in sin or hypocrisy, when we go the way whence we shall not return, it will be a release from prison, and an entrance into everlasting happiness.

Job appeals to God (verses 1–9)

Job reflected on his friends' harsh judgments and, considering himself near death, appealed to God.

Our time on earth is coming to an end.

We should use its remaining days wisely, preparing for eternity.

The righteous should learn from Job's troubles, whether they came from God, from enemies or from friends.

Instead of becoming discouraged from serving God because Job, his faithful servant, was treated so severely, believers should become more determined to persevere.

Those who keep heaven as their destination will keep their feet on the path of faith, whatever hardships or discouragements meet them along the way.

Job looks beyond earthly recovery (verses 10–16)

Job's friends tried to comfort him by predicting a return to worldly prosperity.

But it is unwise to offer comfort grounded entirely in the possibility that earthly circumstances may improve.

We should encourage ourselves and others through the promises of God, his love and grace, and a well-founded hope of eternal life—comforts that cannot fail.

Job learned to make peace with the thought of the grave.

Believers can be willing to die because, in one sense, death is like going to bed after a long day.

They are tired, and it is time to rest.

Why should they refuse when their Father calls them?

Our bodies are already linked to decay, worms and dust.

Let us seek the living hope that will be fulfilled when the wicked person's false hope has disappeared into darkness.

While our bodies rest in the grave, our souls may enjoy the rest God has reserved for his people.

Chapter 17
Chapter Outline
Job appeals from man to God. | (1-9) |
His hope is not in life, but in death. | (10-16) |
Verses 1-9
Job reflects upon the harsh censures his friends had passed upon him, and, looking on himself as a dying man, he appeals to God. Our time is ending. It concerns us carefully to redeem the days of time, and to spend them in getting ready for eternity. We see the good use the righteous should make of Job's afflictions from God, from enemies, and from friends. Instead of being discouraged in the service of God, by the hard usage this faithful servant of God met with, they should be made bold to proceed and persevere therein. Those who keep their eye upon heaven as their end, will keep their feet in the paths of religion as their way, whatever difficulties and discouragements they may meet with.
[Job.17.10-Job.17.16]
Verses 10-16
Job's friends had pretended to comfort him with the hope of his return to a prosperous estate; he here shows that those do not go wisely about the work of comforting the afflicted, who fetch their comforts from the possibility of recovery in this world. It is our wisdom to comfort ourselves, and others, in distress, with that which will not fail; the promise of God, his love and grace, and a well-grounded hope of eternal life. See how Job reconciles himself to the grave. Let this make believers willing to die; it is but going to bed; they are weary, and it is time that they were in their beds. Why should not they go willingly when their Father calls them? Let us remember our bodies are allied to corruption, the worm and the dust; and let us seek for that lively hope which shall be fulfilled, when the hope of the wicked shall be put out in darkness; that when our bodies are in the grave, our souls may enjoy the rest reserved for the people of God.

Bildad had previously given Job some useful counsel and encouragement.

Bildad described the misery of wicked people.

Much of his teaching is true when understood as a warning: sin is a dreadful condition, and without repentance it leads to destruction.

But Bildad thought he could easily apply those warnings to Job.

That conclusion was neither safe nor just.

Angry debaters frequently classify their opponents as enemies of God and draw false conclusions from important truths.

Bildad pictured the wicked person as an animal trapped in a snare or a criminal brought into custody.

From the beginning Satan has been both a murderer and a robber.

He sets traps for sinners wherever they go.

If he makes people sinful like himself, he also makes them miserable like himself.

He hunts for their precious lives.

A wicked person's own transgression becomes a trap, and God prepares judgment for that wrongdoing.

See how sinners run into traps they themselves have made possible.

Bildad described judgment awaiting wicked people in the world to come, a judgment sometimes anticipated in this life.

Sin leads to fear and everlasting confusion.

The terrors of a guilty conscience can be foretastes of that end, as seen in Cain and Judas.

The death of an unrepentant sinner is miserable, even if the person once lived confidently.

At death, every earthly support fails.

How blessed are the saints, and how indebted to Jesus Christ!

Through him death's terror has been so transformed that death becomes a servant and even a friend to the believer.

Bildad described the destruction of wicked people's households and children.

The memory of the righteous brings blessing, while the wicked person's name decays (Proverbs 10:7).

May these warnings encourage sinners to flee from coming wrath, which human strength, cunning and wealth cannot escape.

But Jesus lives forever to deliver everyone who trusts him.

The ruin of the wicked. | (11-21) |
Verses 1-4
Bildad had before given Job good advice and encouragement; here he used nothing but rebukes, and declared his ruin. And he concluded that Job shut out the providence of God from the management of human affairs, because he would not admit himself to be wicked.
[Job.18.5-Job.18.10]
Verses 5-10
Bildad describes the miserable condition of a wicked man; in which there is much certain truth, if we consider that a sinful condition is a sad condition, and that sin will be men's ruin, if they do not repent. Though Bildad thought the application of it to Job was easy, yet it was not safe nor just. It is common for angry disputants to rank their opponents among God's enemies, and to draw wrong conclusions from important truths. The destruction of the wicked is foretold. That destruction is represented under the similitude of a beast or bird caught in a snare, or a malefactor taken into custody. Satan, as he was a murderer, so he was a robber, from the beginning. He, the tempter, lays snares for sinners wherever they go. If he makes them sinful like himself, he will make them miserable like himself. Satan hunts for the precious life. In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare for himself, and God is preparing for his destruction. See here how the sinner runs himself into the snare.
[Job.18.11-Job.18.21]
Verses 11-21
Bildad describes the destruction wicked people are kept for, in the other world, and which in some degree, often seizes them in this world. The way of sin is the way of fear, and leads to everlasting confusion, of which the present terrors of an impure conscience are earnests, as in Cain and Judas. Miserable indeed is a wicked man's death, how secure soever his life was. See him dying; all that he trusts to for his support shall be taken from him. How happy are the saints, and how indebted to the lord Jesus, by whom death is so far done away and changed, that this king of terrors is become a friend and a servant! See the wicked man's family sunk and cut off. His children shall perish, either with him or after him. Those who consult the true honour of their family, and its welfare, will be afraid of withering all by sin. The judgments of God follow the wicked man after death in this world, as a proof of the misery his soul is in after death, and as an earnest of that everlasting shame and contempt to which he shall rise in the great day. The memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot, [Prov.10.7] Pr 10:7. It would be well if this report of wicked men would cause any to flee from the wrath to come, from which their power, policy, and riches cannot deliver them. But Jesus ever liveth to deliver all who trust in him. Bear up then, suffering believers. Ye shall for a little time have sorrow, but your Beloved, your Saviour, will see you again; your hearts shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh away.

Job grieves over his friends' harshness (verses 1–7)

Job's friends condemned him as wicked because of his suffering.

Job described how cruelly they treated him and how his words deserved more understanding than their criticism allowed.

Harsh words from friends add great weight to already painful troubles.

Yet we should be careful not to let those words produce resentment in our hearts.

Look instead to Jesus Christ, who endured hostile sinners speaking against him and was treated with far greater cruelty than Job or we have suffered.

Job describes his abandonment (verses 8–22)

How painful Job's complaints sound!

What makes hell dreadful is the wrath of God.

People whose consciences have become hardened may feel no fear of it now, but they will experience it later.

Those whose consciences have been enlightened fear that judgment now, yet through Christ they will not experience it in eternity.

We must not assume that people whom God afflicts are therefore being treated as his enemies.

Every created thing affects us as God's Providence permits it.

But that truth does not excuse the cruelty of Job's relatives and friends.

Human friendship is uncertain.

If God is our Friend, however, he will never fail us in the hour of need.

Our bodies remain vulnerable to diseases arising within them, however much care we take.

Job appealed to his friends for compassion and rightly criticized their harshness.

It is deeply distressing for someone who loves God to lose both earthly comforts and the inward feeling of God's consolation.

Yet even such suffering does not weaken the evidence that a true believer is a child of God and an heir of glory.

Job confesses faith in his living Redeemer (verses 23–29)

At this point the Spirit of God seems to have worked powerfully within Job.

He made a beautiful confession of faith and expressed sure hope.

His words are full of Christ and heaven.

They show that he sought a better homeland, a heavenly one.

God had taught Job to trust in a living Redeemer, to expect the resurrection of the dead and to look for the life of the world to come.

These hopes comforted him.

Job believed this Redeemer would free sinners from Satan's power and sin's condemnation.

He trusted that the Redeemer was his own Redeemer and expected salvation through him.

He believed the Redeemer was alive already, though he had not yet appeared in human flesh.

At the last day the Redeemer would appear as the world's Judge, raise the dead and complete his people's redemption.

How gladly Job spoke of this hope!

May the Holy Spirit engrave these truths deeply upon our hearts.

We all need to make sure that the root of true religion is in us.

It is a living, strengthening, governing work of grace in the heart—necessary to faith as the root is necessary to a tree's stability and fruitfulness.

Job and his friends disagreed about the ways of Providence.

But they agreed about this root principle: there is another world.

Chapter 19
Chapter Outline
Job complains of unkind usage. | (1-7) |
God was the Author of his afflictions. | (8-22) |
Job's belief in the resurrection. | (23-29) |
Verses 1-7
Job's friends blamed him as a wicked man, because he was so afflicted; here he describes their unkindness, showing that what they condemned was capable of excuse. Harsh language from friends, greatly adds to the weight of afflictions: yet it is best not to lay it to heart, lest we harbour resentment. Rather let us look to Him who endured the contradiction of sinners against himself, and was treated with far more cruelty than Job was, or we can be. ( [Job.19.8-Job.19.22] Job 19:8-22)
[Job.19.8-Job.19.22]
Verses 8-22
How doleful are Job's complaints! What is the fire of hell but the wrath of God! Seared consciences will feel it hereafter, but do not fear it now: enlightened consciences fear it now, but shall not feel it hereafter. It is a very common mistake to think that those whom God afflicts he treats as his enemies. Every creature is that to us which God makes it to be; yet this does not excuse Job's relations and friends. How uncertain is the friendship of men! but if God be our Friend, he will not fail us in time of need. What little reason we have to indulge the body, which, after all our care, is consumed by diseases it has in itself. Job recommends himself to the compassion of his friends, and justly blames their harshness. It is very distressing to one who loves God, to be bereaved at once of outward comfort and of inward consolation; yet if this, and more, come upon a believer, it does not weaken the proof of his being a child of God and heir of glory.
[Job.19.23-Job.19.29]
Verses 23-29
The Spirit of God, at this time, seems to have powerfully wrought on the mind of Job. Here he witnessed a good confession; declared the soundness of his faith, and the assurance of his hope. Here is much of Christ and heaven; and he that said such things are these, declared plainly that he sought the better country, that is, the heavenly. Job was taught of God to believe in a living Redeemer; to look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the world to come; he comforted himself with the expectation of these. Job was assured, that this Redeemer of sinners from the yoke of Satan and the condemnation of sin, was his Redeemer, and expected salvation through him; and that he was a living Redeemer, though not yet come in the flesh; and that at the last day he would appear as the Judge of the world, to raise the dead, and complete the redemption of his people. With what pleasure holy Job enlarges upon this! May these faithful sayings be engraved by the Holy Spirit upon our hearts. We are all concerned to see that the root of the matter be in us. A living, quickening, commanding principle of grace in the heart, is the root of the matter; as necessary to our religion as the root of the tree, to which it owes both its fixedness and its fruitfulness. Job and his friends differed concerning the methods of Providence, but they agreed in the root of the matter, the belief of another world.

Zophar says sinful joy is brief (verses 1–9)

Zophar spoke about the certain misery awaiting the wicked.

The apparent triumph of evil people and the happiness of hypocrites do not last.

Sinful pleasures and gains bring suffering, regret and pain.

They ultimately end in remorse, distress and destruction.

Pretended religion adds hypocrisy to other wrongdoing, so its guilt and final judgment are greater.

Zophar describes the bitterness of sinful gain (verses 10–22)

Zophar described the dreadful condition of wicked people.

He spoke of sinful bodily desires as the sins of youth.

A sinner may hide cherished sinful pleasures, savoring them secretly as though keeping something sweet beneath the tongue.

But God knows what is in the heart.

He knows what is hidden beneath the tongue and will expose it.

Love of the world and its wealth is sinful when it governs the heart.

Violence and injustice bring divine judgment on individuals, families and nations.

The pleasure of sin becomes bitter poison to the person who embraced it.

The same is true of unlawful wealth.

Even in the midst of abundance, wicked people may experience distress because their minds are filled with anxiety.

It is a great mercy when God's sanctifying grace leads someone to return what was unjustly gained, as Zacchaeus did.

But when the horror of a despairing conscience forces restitution, as with Judas, the act brings no true comfort or spiritual benefit.

Zophar announces the wicked person's judgment (verses 23–29)

After describing the suffering produced by wicked conduct, Zophar described the ruin brought by God's judgment.

Only Christ protects against that storm, as the refuge promised in Isaiah 32:2.

Zophar concluded that this was the divinely appointed portion of a wicked person.

Henry's verdict is striking: never was a doctrine better explained or worse applied.

Zophar intended to prove Job a hypocrite, though he had no grounds for doing so.

We should receive the sound warning and apply it to ourselves, learning reverence and turning from sin.

One true sight of Jesus, opened and impressed upon us by the Holy Spirit, can quiet a thousand sinful questions about why believers suffer.

The ruin of the wicked. | (10-22) |
The portion of the wicked. | (23-29) |
Verses 1-9
Zophar's discourse is upon the certain misery of the wicked. The triumph of the wicked and the joy of the hypocrite are fleeting. The pleasures and gains of sin bring disease and pain; they end in remorse, anguish, and ruin. Dissembled piety is double iniquity, and the ruin that attends it will be accordingly.
[Job.20.10-Job.20.22]
Verses 10-22
The miserable condition of the wicked man in this world is fully set forth. The lusts of the flesh are here called the sins of his youth. His hiding it and keeping it under his tongue, denotes concealment of his beloved lust, and delight therein. But He who knows what is in the heart, knows what is under the tongue, and will discover it. The love of the world, and of the wealth of it, also is wickedness, and man sets his heart upon these. Also violence and injustice, these sins bring God's judgments upon nations and families. Observe the punishment of the wicked man for these things. Sin is turned into gall, than which nothing is more bitter; it will prove to him poison; so will all unlawful gains be. In his fulness he shall be in straits, through the anxieties of his own mind. To be led by the sanctifying grace of God to restore what was unjustly gotten, as Zaccheus was, is a great mercy. But to be forced to restore by the horrors of a despairing conscience, as Judas was, has no benefit and comfort attending it.
[Job.20.23-Job.20.29]
Verses 23-29
Zophar, having described the vexations which attend wicked practices, shows their ruin from God's wrath. There is no fence against this, but in Christ, who is the only Covert from the storm and tempest, [Isa.32.2] Is 32:2. Zophar concludes, "This is the portion of a wicked man from God;" it is allotted him. Never was any doctrine better explained, or worse applied, than this by Zophar, who intended to prove Job a hypocrite. Let us receive the good explanation, and make a better application, for warning to ourselves, to stand in awe and sin not. One view of Jesus, directed by the Holy Spirit, and by him suitably impressed upon our souls, will quell a thousand carnal reasonings about the suffering of the faithful.
